title: GreyNoise traces an AI-agent swarm that breached 395 organizations via PaperCut in four hours
subtitle: A Russian-speaking operator ran hundreds of Codex and DeepSeek-driven agents against two fresh PaperCut CVEs, hitting 11 orgs in the first 26 seconds and 440 servers across 48 countries.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: GreyNoise published its analysis of a coordinated AI-agent attack campaign on September 10, 2026. The operator — GreyNoise assesses them as likely Russian-speaking — used hundreds of AI agents built on OpenAI's Codex harness and a DeepSeek model to exploit two PaperCut NG/MF vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-81578 and CVE-2026-82078, for which PaperCut had issued emergency patches on August 28. The campaign reached its first remote code execution in under four hours, achieved first domain admin two hours after that, and once the full swarm launched compromised at least eleven organizations in twenty-six seconds. Final scope: 440 PaperCut instances at 395 identified victim organizations across 48 countries. Education was the hardest-hit sector by a wide margin, with 204 victims.

The mechanism is the story. This was not a single exploit script run against many targets. It was a fleet of language-model agents, each capable of adapting to a target and driving a multi-step compromise, orchestrated from a single command endpoint at 45.142.193.132. The attacker used AI to develop the exploits against the CVEs and then again to operate them at scale. The gap between patch release and mass exploitation compressed to under two weeks, and the wall-clock cost of running four hundred parallel intrusions dropped to whatever the API bill was.

This confirms a pattern security researchers have been warning about since 2024: agent economics change the shape of the threat model. Vulnerability-to-mass-exploitation windows that used to take weeks — because a human had to write, test, and deploy the tooling — now collapse. That interacts poorly with the fact that many enterprise patch cycles still assume a slower adversary. The Five Eyes agencies flagged this exact scenario in June; this campaign is the first well-documented instance of it running against a real product line.

For learners, particularly those going into security or IT: agent-driven offense is not theoretical anymore. If you administer software, assume the delta between a CVE dropping and a swarm hitting your instance is measured in days, not weeks. If you build tools, build with the assumption that whatever developer harness you ship — Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, or anything else — will be pointed at your users and their servers by someone. Defensive AI has to move at the same speed the offensive side just demonstrated, and that gap is where a lot of the next few years of security work will happen.
